section.para:
This tutorial offers a quick overview of bali-phy with an emphasis on concrete analysis of real datasets. Other documentation includes:
The User Guide is much more complete. Run tool --help to see command line options for tool. Run man tool to see the manual page for tool. Manual pages for bali-phy and tools are also available online.
Before you start this tutorial, please download and install bali-phy, following the installation instructions in the User Guide.

The shell commands below work in bash and zsh on Linux and macOS. On Windows, use WSL for this tutorial; see the User Guide's installation instructions. The % marks the shell prompt and is not part of the command.

The analyses below are exercises, not a guarantee of convergence. You can run bpy-summarize while the analyses continue to check their progress. Before using results for inference, assess convergence and effective sample sizes as described in the User Guide.

Go to your home directory: % cd ~ Make a directory called alignment_files inside it: % mkdir alignment_files Go into the alignment_files directory: % cd alignment_files Download the example alignment files: % wget https://www.bali-phy.org/examples.tgz Alternatively, you can use curl % curl -O https://www.bali-phy.org/examples.tgz Extract the compressed archive: % tar -zxf examples.tgz Take a look inside the examples directory: % ls examples Take a look at an input file (you can press 'q' to exit 'less'): % less examples/5S-rRNA/5d.fasta Get some information about the alignment: % alignment-info examples/5S-rRNA/5d.fasta

What version of bali-phy are you running? When was it compiled? Which compiler? For what computer type? % bali-phy -v % bali-phy --version Look at the list of command line options: % bali-phy -h | less % bali-phy --help | less % bali-phy help | less By default, not all the options are shown. To see more options, try: % bali-phy help advanced | less % bali-phy help expert | less
All bali-phy tools also take --help. % alignment-thin --help | less % alignment-cat --help | less

You can also get help on models, distributions, functions, and command-line options: % bali-phy help TN93 | less # Tamura-Nei (1993) model % bali-phy help Normal | less # Normal distribution % bali-phy help quantile | less # quantile function
You can find out which models, distributions, and functions are available: % bali-phy help models | less # What models are available? % bali-phy help distributions | less # What distributions are available? % bali-phy help functions | less # What functions are available?
You can get extended help on each command line option: % bali-phy help iterations | less # --iterations=<num> command line option % bali-phy help alphabet | less # --alphabet=<a> command line option

info.title: Analysis 1: 5S rRNA -- free alignment versus fixed alignment

section.para: Let's estimate a phylogeny on a very small data set under both a free alignment and a fixed alignment to see how the alignment affects our confidence in the estimated topology.
section.section:
Free alignment
Let's get started by going to the examples directory: % cd ~/alignment_files/examples/5S-rRNA
Now let's start a run. % bali-phy 5d-clustalw.fasta --smodel 'GTR +> ASRV.Gamma(4) +> Inv' --name 5d-freeA &
You have started the first copy of the analysis. BAli-Phy will create a directory called 5d-freeA-1 to hold output files from this analysis, as directed by the --name 5d-freeA option.
Let's run another copy of the same analysis: % bali-phy 5d-clustalw.fasta --smodel 'GTR +> ASRV.Gamma(4) +> Inv' --name 5d-freeA &
This command will create another directory called 5d-freeA-2 for its own output files. This additional run will take advantage of a second processor. It will also allow us to determine if the two runs have performed enough iterations to agree.
You can take a look at jobs running in the background. There should be two bali-phy jobs running: % jobs The previous command only shows jobs started by the shell you are typing in. You can also examine all processes running on your computer. bali-phy should show up near the top since it is using a lot of the CPU: % top # press 'q' to exit top In order to see how many iterations have completed, check the number of lines in the log files: % wc -l 5d-freeA-*/C1.log To summarize the results generated so far, run the summary script and then view the results in a web browser: % bpy-summarize 5d-freeA-1/ 5d-freeA-2/
Open Results/index.html in your web browser.
For this exercise, collect about 2000 iterations from each run, then summarize the latest results: % wc -l 5d-freeA-*/C1.log % bpy-summarize 5d-freeA-1/ 5d-freeA-2/ % mv Results 5d-freeA.Results
Open 5d-freeA.Results/index.html in your web browser. Now let's kill the bali-phy processes: % top # use top to find the PID (process id) for each of the bali-phy processes % kill pid1 % kill pid2 % top # check that the jobs have stopped. If FigTree is installed, you can also examine the tree with it: % figtree 5d-freeA.Results/c50.PP.tree &
When it says "Please select a name for these values", enter PP. Then, enable "Branch Labels". Under "Branch Labels / Display", select "PP". You can increase the font size to make the figure more readable. You can also increase the font size of the tip labels.
Parameter questions:
What is the meaning of Inv:pInv parameter? (Run bali-phy help Inv) What is the prior distribution on Inv:pInv? (See Model and priors / Substitution model) What is the posterior median for Inv:pInv? (See Scalar Variables)
Alignment questions:
Which part of the alignment is most uncertain? (See Alignment Distribution: follow an AU link for a consensus alignment)
Tree questions (free alignment):
How many internal branches are in the 50% consensus tree? What is the posterior probability for each of these internal branches?

Fixed alignment % cd ~/alignment_files/examples/5S-rRNA % bali-phy 5d-clustalw.fasta -S 'GTR +> ASRV.Gamma(4) +> Inv' -I none -n 5d-fixedA & % bali-phy 5d-clustalw.fasta -S 'GTR +> ASRV.Gamma(4) +> Inv' -I none -n 5d-fixedA & The -I none is a short form of --imodel=none, where imodel means the insertion-deletion model. When there's no model of insertions and deletions, then the alignment must be kept fixed.
Summarize the results while the analyses run. For this exercise, collect about 2000 iterations from each run before comparing the fixed and free alignments: % wc -l 5d-fixedA-*/C1.log % bpy-summarize 5d-fixedA-1/ 5d-fixedA-2
Examine the majority consensus tree for the fixed alignment analysis: % figtree Results/c50.PP.tree &
Tree questions (fixed alignment):
How many internal branches are in the 50% consensus tree? What is the posterior probability for each of these internal branches? For this data set, how does fixing the alignment affect our confidence in the tree? Why might this be?
Stop these two runs when you have finished, using their process IDs as in the free-alignment example.

article.section:
Analysis 2: ITS sequences -- multi-gene analysis
Let's do an analysis of intergenic transcribed spacer (ITS) genes from 20 specimens of lichenized fungi (Gaya et al, 2011 analyzes 68 specimens). The ITS genes contain a lot of variation, but are hard to align. This analysis will show how to estimate the alignment, phylogeny, and evolutionary parameters using MCMC. Averaging over all alignments makes it safe to use the ITS region without throwing out ambiguously-aligned regions.
This data set is divided into three gene regions, or partitions. It is assumed that all genes evolve on the same tree, but may have different rates and evolutionary parameters. Let's look at the sequences. How long are they? % cd ~/alignment_files/examples/ITS % alignment-info ITS1.fasta % alignment-info 5.8S.fasta % alignment-info ITS2.fasta
By default, each gene gets a default substitution model based on whether it contains DNA/RNA or amino acids. By running bali-phy with the --test option, we can reveal what substitution models and priors will be used, without actually starting a run. % bali-phy ITS1.fasta 5.8S.fasta ITS2.fasta --test
Let's run two copies of this analysis: % bali-phy ITS1.fasta 5.8S.fasta ITS2.fasta & % bali-phy ITS1.fasta 5.8S.fasta ITS2.fasta & Since we did not specify a name for the analysis, bali-phy creates the name ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 from the input file names.
Let's analyze the results, even if the analysis has not yet converged: % bpy-summarize ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-1/ ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-2/
Open Results/index.html in your web browser.
The optional program Tracer graphically displays the posterior probability distribution for each parameter. % tracer ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-1/C1.log ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-2/C1.log & If you are using Windows or Mac, first run Tracer, and then press the + button to add the files.
Questions about parameter differences between genes These genes have different evolutionary processes. How does the evolutionary process for these genes differ in:
substitution rate? (scale1, scale2, ...) insertion-deletion rate? (I1/RS07:rate, I2/RS07:rate, ...) nucleotide frequencies? (S1/TN93:pi[A], S1/TN93:pi[C], ... ) number of indels? (#indels)

Analysis 3: Exons and Introns Let's look at a data set containing both exons and introns. The pattern of dividing a sequence into high-rate and low-rate regions also applies to stems and loops in RNA sequences. It is helpful to allow different insertion-deletion rates in conserved and non-conserved regions of a gene.
Extracting parts of a gene First, let's split the gene into separate FASTA files for each intron and exon: % cd ~/alignment_files/examples/ferns/ % alignment-cat -c 5-8 -e cleaned.fasta > exon1.fasta % alignment-cat -c 9-453 -e cleaned.fasta > intron1.fasta % alignment-cat -c 454-596 -e cleaned.fasta > exon2.fasta % alignment-cat -c 597-864 -e cleaned.fasta > intron2.fasta % alignment-cat -c 865-948 -e cleaned.fasta > exon3.fasta % alignment-cat -c 949-1328 -e cleaned.fasta > intron3.fasta % alignment-cat -c 1329-1393 -e cleaned.fasta > exon4.fasta Now, let's put the pieces back together in case we need the complete gene in the future: % alignment-cat exon1.fasta intron1.fasta exon2.fasta intron2.fasta exon3.fasta intron3.fasta exon4.fasta > combined.fasta It is also possible to refer to character sets without creating a file for each one, as mentioned below.
The ASRV.Free model
We will add -S 'GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4)' to use the free-rates model of substitution with 4 categories: % bali-phy exon1.fasta intron1.fasta exon2.fasta intron2.fasta exon3.fasta intron3.fasta exon4.fasta -S 'GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4)' --test This model is more general than ASRV.Gamma, since it estimates 4 free rates and the frequencies of the 4 rates. These 8 parameters have 6 degrees of freedom, which is a lot more than the 1 degree of freedom for the ASRV.Gamma model. Furthermore, each partition by default gets a separate copy of the model, which leads to 42 degrees of freedom just for the ASRV.Free part of the model!
Fixing the alignment of some partitions
We will now add -I 1,3,5,7:none to disable alignment estimation, but only for the exons: % bali-phy exon1.fasta intron1.fasta exon2.fasta intron2.fasta exon3.fasta intron3.fasta exon4.fasta -S 'GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4)' -I 1,3,5,7:none --test
Linking parameters between partitions We can reduce the number of parameters by using one set of parameters for the exons, and one set for the introns. This is called linking the models. % bali-phy exon1.fasta intron1.fasta exon2.fasta intron2.fasta exon3.fasta intron3.fasta exon4.fasta -I 1,3,5,7:none -S '1,3,5,7:GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4)' -S '2,4,6:GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4)' --test We would also like to share the indel model between introns: % bali-phy exon1.fasta intron1.fasta exon2.fasta intron2.fasta exon3.fasta intron3.fasta exon4.fasta -I 1,3,5,7:none -S '1,3,5,7:GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4)' -S '2,4,6:GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4)' -I 2,4,6: --test
Character sets
Instead of creating separate files for each intron and exon, we can also refer to character sets of the combined file: % bali-phy cleaned.fasta:5-8 cleaned.fasta:454-596 cleaned.fasta:865-948 cleaned.fasta:1329-1393 cleaned.fasta:9-453 cleaned.fasta:597-864 cleaned.fasta:949-1328 -I 1,2,3,4:none -S '1,2,3,4:GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4)' -S '5,6,7:GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4)' -I 5,6,7: --test However, the command line is getting so long that it is difficult to manage.
Option files
Instead of writing all options on the command line, we can put some of them into a text file that is easier to manage and edit. Let's make a text file called options1.txt: # exon1 :align cleaned.fasta:5-8 # intron1 :align cleaned.fasta:9-453 # exon2 :align cleaned.fasta:454-596 # intron2 :align cleaned.fasta:597-864 # exon3 :align cleaned.fasta:865-948 # intron3 :align cleaned.fasta:949-1328 # exon4 :align cleaned.fasta:1329-1393
# exons :smodel 1,3,5,7:GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4) :imodel 1,3,5,7:none
# introns :smodel 2,4,6:GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4) :imodel 2,4,6:
We can then run % bali-phy -c options1.txt --test
Let's run two copies of this analysis: % bali-phy -c options1.txt & % bali-phy -c options1.txt &
Questions about intron alignments
How do bali-phy alignments of the introns differ from muscle and mafft alignments of the introns? How much certainty or uncertainty do the intron alignments have? How do the evolutionary rates of the exons compare to the evolutionary rates of the introns? Would it be reasonable to link the intron rates? How about the exon rates?
Exons as codons + introns as nucleotides Another thing that we can do is to use a codon model on the combined exons, while using a nucleotide model on the introns. In order to load nucleotide sequences as codons, three conditions must be met:
Sequence lengths must be multiples of three.
AAA --- TTT is OK
AAA --- T-- is not OK.
Gaps must be codon-aligned.
AAA --- TTT is OK
AA- --A TT- is not OK.
The sequences must be in-frame and not have stop codons.
ATG AAT AAA is OK, because it translates to MNK.
AAT GAA TAA is not OK, because it translates to NE*, where * is a stop codon.
Note that spaces in FASTA files are allowed, but not required.
Let's first extract the coding data: % alignment-cat exon{1,2,3,4}.fasta -c2-295 > coding.fasta # Concatenate exons and chop off partial codons at beginning and end % sed '/^>/!s/-/N/g' coding.fasta > coding-with-N.fasta # Replace gaps in sequences, preserving FASTA names % mv coding-with-N.fasta coding.fasta We can then construct an option file options2.txt: :align intron1.fasta :align intron2.fasta :align intron3.fasta :align coding.fasta
:smodel 1,2,3:GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4) :imodel 1,2,3:RS07
:smodel 4:GY94 #:smodel 4:GY94_ext(GTR_sym) # A GTR-based version of GY94 a.k.a. M0. #:smodel 4:GTR +> FMutSel0 #:smodel 4:|w:FMutSel0(omega=w)| +> M3 :imodel 4:none
We can choose any one of the three codon models for the coding sequences in the 4th partition. % bali-phy -c options2.txt --test Try changing the model to GTR +> FMutSel0. Does the number of parameters increase or decrease?
Exons as amino acids + introns as nucleotides We can also translate the coding sequence into a protein sequence, while using a nucleotide model on the introns. Let's first extract the coding data: % alignment-translate < coding.fasta > protein.fasta
We can then construct an option file options3.txt: :align intron1.fasta :align intron2.fasta :align intron3.fasta :align protein.fasta
:smodel 1,2,3:GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=4) :imodel 1,2,3:RS07
:smodel 4:LG +> ASRV.LogNormal(n=4) :imodel 4:none
% bali-phy -c options3.txt --test

Analysis 4: ITS sequences - with a better model
Let's revisit the ITS sequences used in analysis 2. Now that you've been exposed to different models in different partitions, let's use a more complex substitution model for the ITS partitions (--smodel '1,3:TN93 +> ASRV.Free(n=3)'). Note that this also links the substitution models for the ITS partitions.
We can also fix the alignment for the 5.8S partition, since it has almost no indels. Return to the ITS directory and save the following options as options4.txt: % cd ~/alignment_files/examples/ITS
:align ITS1.fasta :align 5.8S.fasta :align ITS2.fasta
:smodel 1,3:TN93 +> ASRV.Free(n=3) :smodel 2:TN93
:imodel 2:none
:scale 1,3:
% bali-phy -c options4.txt --test
This file additionally links the scale for the two ITS partitions (--scale=1,3:). This forces them to share the same evolutionary rate, and allows more precise estimates of the shared scale. You can run the analysis with unlinked scales by removing this option in order to determine if (i) the scales are similar enough to share and (ii) the scales have a high enough variance that they need to be linked.

section.para: While those analyses are running, let's look at how to specify more complex substitution models in bali-phy.

When you don't specify values for parameters like imodel, bali-phy uses sensible defaults. For example, these two commands are equivalent: % cd ~/alignment_files/examples/ % bali-phy 5S-rRNA/25-muscle.fasta --test % bali-phy 5S-rRNA/25-muscle.fasta --test --alphabet=RNA --smodel=TN93 --imodel=RS07 You can change the substitution model from the Tamura-Nei model to the General Time-Reversible model: % bali-phy 5S-rRNA/25-muscle.fasta --test -S GTR Here the -S GTR is a short form of --smodel=GTR, where smodel means the substitution model.

You can also allow different sites to evolve at 5 different rates using the ASRV.Gamma(4) + Inv model of rate heterogeneity: % bali-phy 5S-rRNA/25-muscle.fasta --test -S 'GTR +> ASRV.Gamma(4) +> Inv' You can also use ASRV.LogNormal instead of ASRV.Gamma. ASRV.LogNormal+Inv is sometimes better behaved than ASRV.Gamma+Inv, because the smallest rate bin under ASRV.LogNormal is not quite as close to 0. % bali-phy 5S-rRNA/25-muscle.fasta --test -S 'GTR +> ASRV.LogNormal(4) +> Inv' You can allow 5 different rates that are all independently estimated: % bali-phy 5S-rRNA/25-muscle.fasta --test -S 'GTR +> ASRV.Free(n=5)'

Heterotachy occurs when the evolutionary rate changes across the tree. One version of heterotachy is the Tuffley-Steel (1998) model, where each state alternates between an ON and OFF state. % bali-phy 5S-rRNA/25-muscle.fasta --test -S 'GTR +> Covarion.TuffleySteel98' The Huelsenbeck (2002) model allows combining rate variation with Tuffley-Steel heterotachy: % bali-phy 5S-rRNA/25-muscle.fasta --test -S 'GTR +> ASRV.Gamma +> Covarion.Huelsenbeck02' You can also use the Huelsenbeck model with the free-rates model: % bali-phy 5S-rRNA/25-muscle.fasta --test -S 'GTR +> ASRV.Free +> Covarion.Huelsenbeck02'

section.section:
Codon models and selection
We will analyze myxovirus resistance (Mx) genes from ten mammals and two birds, using sequences from Álvarez-Carretero et al. (2023). See Mx/README.md in the examples for the citation, provenance, and preprocessing details. The terminal stop codons have been removed; the remaining alignment contains 663 codon columns. % cd ~/alignment_files/examples/Mx
We first condition on this alignment using -I none. The single-ω and site analyses still estimate the tree topology. Later we will fix the topology for branch analyses, and finally revisit the site test while estimating the alignment. These Bayesian analyses use different models and methods from the original PAML tutorial; their numerical results need not match exactly.
The commands below start MCMC runs for an analysis. In contrast, adding --test checks the model setup without performing an analysis. Run two independent copies of each analysis, as in the earlier alignment exercises, and check agreement and effective sample sizes before interpreting the results. Work through the examples one at a time; there is no need to run all of them simultaneously. See the User Guide's analysis instructions for convergence and burn-in guidance.
One ω for the whole sequence
Start with one ω shared across sites and branches. GTR describes nucleotide mutation; MNM allows changes of more than one nucleotide within a codon; MutSelAA estimates amino-acid preferences shared across sites; and dNdS adds the ω multiplier. Here ω describes nonsynonymous change beyond the effect of these preferences, not a raw ratio of observed changes. % bali-phy Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta -A Codons -I none -S 'GTR +> MNM +> MutSelAA +> dNdS' --name Mx-single-fixedA & % bali-phy Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta -A Codons -I none -S 'GTR +> MNM +> MutSelAA +> dNdS' --name Mx-single-fixedA &
These commands create Mx-single-fixedA-1 and Mx-single-fixedA-2 in a fresh working directory. Summarize the runs: % bpy-summarize Mx-single-fixedA-1/ Mx-single-fixedA-2/ % mv Results Mx-single-fixedA.Results
Open Mx-single-fixedA.Results/index.html. Read the ω estimate and credible interval in the parameter report. A single ω averages across the sequence and cannot identify selected sites. You can summarize while the runs continue, but a report's existence does not establish convergence. Repeat the summary after collecting more samples as needed; move aside the previous named report before using the same destination again. Stop the runs using the process-control instructions from the earlier exercises when finished.
The remaining examples each show one launch command. Run it twice to create the two independent run directories used by the summary command. If you already have runs with the same name, BAli-Phy chooses higher suffixes; substitute the actual directories. Combine runs of the same model and settings, not runs from different examples.
Different ω values among sites
M8a allows a distribution of ω values below one and an additional category with ω equal to one. It describes variation among sites without allowing a positive-selection category. The expression |w:...| builds the codon model for each supplied ω; the mutation parameters and amino-acid preferences are shared across categories. % bali-phy Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta -A Codons -I none -S '|w:GTR +> MNM +> MutSelAA +> dNdS(omega=w)| +> M8a' --name Mx-M8a-fixedA &
Run this command twice, then summarize: % bpy-summarize Mx-M8a-fixedA-1/ Mx-M8a-fixedA-2/ % mv Results Mx-M8a-fixedA.Results
Open Mx-M8a-fixedA.Results/index.html and examine the site-model parameters and category proportions. This analysis estimates variation in ω; it does not compare a selection hypothesis with a no-selection hypothesis.
Testing for positively selected sites
M8a_test compares M8a with M8, whose additional category has ω above one. Both hypotheses are included in one analysis: you do not need to fit M8a and M8 separately to perform this test. % bali-phy Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta -A Codons -I none -S '|w:GTR +> MNM +> MutSelAA +> dNdS(omega=w)| +> M8a_test' --name Mx-M8a-test-fixedA &
Run this command twice, then summarize: % bpy-summarize Mx-M8a-test-fixedA-1/ Mx-M8a-test-fixedA-2/ % mv Results Mx-M8a-test-fixedA.Results
Open Mx-M8a-test-fixedA.Results/index.html. Under Positive selection, find Support for positive selection in the model. This reports posterior support and log odds for the selection hypothesis. Use this dedicated table to assess model support. See the User Guide for the relation between posterior odds, prior odds, and Bayes factors.
Then examine the site probabilities. Overall posterior averages over both hypotheses; Posterior with selection conditions on the selection hypothesis. A high conditional probability at a codon is not by itself strong overall evidence if the selection hypothesis has little support. In the alignment viewer, select posSelection; these views are labelled Model-averaged and Conditional on positiveSelectionInModel.
Different ω values among branches
Now ask whether the terminal chicken and duck branches have a different ω from the remaining branches. The supplied Mx_foreground.tree labels both with :[&foreground=1]; unlabelled branches use category 0. The two bird branches share one ω, and the ancestral branch leading to birds is not labelled. The annotation follows a colon because it belongs to the branch, not the node.
Fix the supplied topology so these branch groups remain defined. Branch lengths are still estimated. BranchModel uses one ω per group, shared across sites: % bali-phy Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta -A Codons -I none --fix topology=Mx_foreground.tree -S '|w:GTR +> MNM +> MutSelAA +> dNdS(omega=w)| +> BranchModel' --name Mx-branch-fixedA &
Run this command twice, then summarize: % bpy-summarize Mx-branch-fixedA-1/ Mx-branch-fixedA-2/ % mv Results Mx-branch-fixedA.Results
Open Mx-branch-fixedA.Results/index.html and find the category ω estimates under Branch models. The categories can differ while both ω values remain below one. This analysis estimates separate values; the next analysis tests whether a separate foreground value is supported.
Testing for a difference between branch groups
For BranchModel_test, use Mx_branch_test.tree. Each bird terminal branch has :[&foreground={0,1}]. The entries specify its category under each hypothesis: hypothesis 0 uses category 0 everywhere; hypothesis 1 assigns a shared category 1 to chicken and duck. Other branches stay in category 0 under both hypotheses. % bali-phy Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta -A Codons -I none --fix topology=Mx_branch_test.tree -S '|w:GTR +> MNM +> MutSelAA +> dNdS(omega=w)| +> BranchModel_test' --name Mx-branch-test-fixedA &
Run this command twice, then summarize: % bpy-summarize Mx-branch-test-fixedA-1/ Mx-branch-test-fixedA-2/ % mv Results Mx-branch-test-fixedA.Results
Open Mx-branch-test-fixedA.Results/index.html. Under Branch models, read Hypothesis support and the ω summaries for each hypothesis. This tests whether the branch groups need different ω values, not specifically whether ω exceeds one. Interpret the posterior support using the manual's model-support guidance linked above.
Testing for selection at some sites on foreground branches
BranchSite is a test, despite having no _test suffix. It allows some sites to have ω above one on foreground branches while their background ω remains at or below one, and compares this with a null hypothesis that fixes their foreground ω to one. Use the scalar foreground=1 labels in Mx_foreground.tree, rather than the hypothesis lists used for BranchModel_test. % bali-phy Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta -A Codons -I none --fix topology=Mx_foreground.tree -S '|w:GTR +> MNM +> MutSelAA +> dNdS(omega=w)| +> BranchSite' --name Mx-branch-site-fixedA &
Run this command twice, then summarize: % bpy-summarize Mx-branch-site-fixedA-1/ Mx-branch-site-fixedA-2/ % mv Results Mx-branch-site-fixedA.Results
Open Mx-branch-site-fixedA.Results/index.html and read Support for positive selection in the model. In the alignment viewer, foreground-posSelection shows selection probabilities for the foreground branches and foreground-dNdS shows ω estimates. The corresponding background-posSelection and background-dNdS properties describe the background branches. Distinguish overall from selection-conditional probabilities as in the site test. Foreground branches should be chosen from the biological question before examining the selection results.
Estimating the alignment along with selection
So far, we have treated the supplied alignment as known. Return to the M8a site test and remove -I none to estimate the alignment jointly with selection. Keep the substitution model and topology treatment the same as in the fixed-alignment site test; the topology is estimated in both analyses. % bali-phy Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta -A Codons -S '|w:GTR +> MNM +> MutSelAA +> dNdS(omega=w)| +> M8a_test' --name Mx-M8a-test-freeA &
Run this command twice, then summarize: % bpy-summarize Mx-M8a-test-freeA-1/ Mx-M8a-test-freeA-2/ % mv Results Mx-M8a-test-freeA.Results
Joint estimation can yield a more accurate alignment and accounts for alignment uncertainty when assessing selection, although improved accuracy is not guaranteed. It adds alignment sampling, so reassess convergence rather than assuming the same run length suffices.
As the alignment changes, the grouping of codons into columns changes too. Selection summaries follow individual codons across sampled alignments instead of treating a fixed column number as a site's identity. Consequently, codons in the same displayed column can have different probabilities. Compare the fixed- and variable-alignment reports' model support, representative alignments, and codon probabilities. Use sequence names and ungapped positions to identify the same codons across reports, rather than matching column numbers.
See the User Guide's discussion of selected codons for details of the site table and alignment display. These comparisons show the effect of alignment treatment; without an independent reference, they do not establish which inferred alignment is more accurate.
A historical codon model
For comparison with older analyses, the Goldman–Yang model with F1x4 frequencies can be specified as follows. Here --test only displays the setup: % bali-phy Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta -A Codons -I none --test -S 'GY94(pi=F1x4)'
This historical model does not include the MNM and amino-acid preference components used above. See the User Guide's background-model discussion for the reasons behind the choices in the worked examples.

section.para: Return to the examples directory: % cd ~/alignment_files/examples/ We can use the TN93+Gamma(4)+Inv model without specifying parameters: % bali-phy Mx/Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta --test -S 'TN93 +> ASRV.Gamma +> Inv' However, we can also fix parameter values: % bali-phy Mx/Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta --test -S 'TN93 +> ASRV.Gamma(n=4,alpha=1) +> Inv(pInv=0.2)' Here we have set the shape parameter for the Gamma distribution to 1, and the fraction of invariant sites to 20%. Since these parameters are fixed, they will not be estimated and their values will not be shown in the log file.
You can see the parameters for a model by using the help command, as in: % bali-phy help ASRV.Gamma This will show the default value or default prior for each parameter, if there is one.

By default the fraction of invariant sites follows a Uniform(0,1) distribution: % bali-phy help Inv However, we can specify an alternative prior: % bali-phy Mx/Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta --test -S 'TN93 +> ASRV.Gamma(n=4) +> Inv(pInv~Uniform(0,0.2))' We can also specify parameters as positional arguments instead of using variable names: % bali-phy Mx/Mx_aln.nonstop.fasta --test -S 'TN93 +> ASRV.Gamma(4) +> Inv(~Uniform(0,0.2))' Here "~" indicates a sample from the uniform distribution instead of the distribution itself.

The insertion-deletion model also has parameters. % bali-phy help RS07 Here the default value for RS07:meanLength is ShiftedExponential(10,1). This indicates a random value that is obtained by sampling an Exponential random variable with mean 10 and then adding 1 to it.

info.title: Specifying the model for each partition

section.para: For analyses with multiple partitions, we might want to use different models for different partitions. When two partitions have the same model, we might also want them to have the same parameters. This is described in more detail in the manual.

Now let's specify different substitution models for different partitions.
% cd ~/alignment_files/examples/ITS % bali-phy {ITS1,5.8S,ITS2}.fasta -S 1:GTR -S 2:HKY85 -S 3:TN93 --test

info.title: Disabling alignment estimation for some partitions

section.para: We can also disable alignment estimation for some, but not all, partitions: % bali-phy {ITS1,5.8S,ITS2}.fasta -I 1:RS07 -I 2:none -I 3:RS07 --test Specifying -I 2:none removes the insertion-deletion model and parameters for partition 2 and also disables alignment estimation for that partition.
Note that there is no longer an I3 indel model. Partition #3 now has the I2 indel model.

We can also specify that some partitions with the same model also share the same parameters for that model: % bali-phy {ITS1,5.8S,ITS2}.fasta -S 1,3:GTR -I 1,3:RS07 -S 2:TN93 -I 2:none --test This means that the information is pooled between the partitions to better estimate the shared parameters.

Take a look at the model parameters, and the parentheticals after the model descriptions. You should see that there is no longer an S3 substitution model or an I3 indel model. Instead, partitions #1 and #3 share the S1 substitution model and the I1 indel model.

We can also specify that some partitions share the same scaling factor for branch lengths: % bali-phy {ITS1,5.8S,ITS2}.fasta -S 1,3:GTR -I 1,3:RS07 -S 2:TN93 -I 2:none --scale=1,3: --test This means that the branch lengths for partitions 1 and 3 are the same, instead of being independently estimated.
Take a look at the model parameters. There is no longer a scale3 parameter. Instead, partitions 1 and 3 share scale1.

section.section:
Splitting and merging Alignments
You might want to split concatenated gene regions: % cd ~/alignment_files/examples/ITS-many/ % alignment-cat -c1-223 ITS-region.fasta > 1.fasta % alignment-cat -c224-379 ITS-region.fasta > 2.fasta % alignment-cat -c380-551 ITS-region.fasta > 3.fasta
Later you might want to put them back together again: % alignment-cat 1.fasta 2.fasta 3.fasta > 123.fasta

section.para:
You might want to reduce the number of taxa while attempting to preserve phylogenetic diversity: % alignment-thin --cutoff=5 ITS-region.fasta --verbose --protect=Csaxicola420 > ITS-region-thinned.fasta This removes sequences with fewer than 5 directional mismatches to the closest other sequence.
The --verbose option shows which sequences are removed and the distance to their closest neighbor. The --protect option keeps specific sequences in the data set.
You can also specify that data sets should be shrunk to a specific number of sequences: % alignment-thin --down-to=30 ITS-region.fasta --verbose > ITS-region-thinned.fasta
To see all options, run: % alignment-thin --help

section.section: Cleaning the data set Keep only sequences that are not too short: % alignment-thin --longer-than=250 ITS-region.fasta > ITS-region-long.fasta Remove 10 sequences with the smallest number of conserved residues: % alignment-thin --remove-gappy=10 ITS-region.fasta > ITS-region-sane.fasta Keep only columns with a minimum number of residues: % alignment-thin --min-letters=5 ITS-region.fasta > ITS-region-censored.fasta
